title: Innovation in Public Toilets under Swachh Bharat Mission
excerpt: An overview of recent public toilet innovations across Indian cities, their relevance for UPSC exams and key points for prelims and mains preparation.
releaseDate: 02 OCT 2026 12:28PM Over the years, India’s cities have made significant strides in expanding access to public sanitation facilities. From improving availability and cleanliness to enhancing safety and accessibility, cities are adopting innovative approaches to make public toilets more inclusive and user-friendly. Building on these efforts, the Swachh Bharat Mission (SBM) , launched on 2 October 2014 , has advanced sanitation innovation across India. Cities built toilets, raised awareness and worked towards becoming Open Defecation Free (ODF) . Many went further, achieving ODF+ and ODF++ status. In 2022, the Toilets 2.0 initiative under Swachh Bharat Mission-Urban (SBM-U) raised the bar again. Its aim was to make Community and Public Toilets (CT/PTs) safe, clean and inviting for everyone. Citizens can now find the nearest facility through the ‘SBM Toilet Locator’ on the Swachhata app. Today, the change is visible in unexpected places. An old bus has become a women's toilet. Plastic waste has turned into building material. A busy market now hosts a smart lounge. A small city has found a safe way to handle sanitary waste. Pilgrim towns offer facilities open to all. Together, these stories trace the journey from basic access to dignity, safety and innovation. New Age Toilets: A Scrap Bus Becomes a Safe Space for Women Women travelling through crowded bus terminals often struggle to find a clean and private toilet. In Bengaluru, Karnataka , an old bus found a new purpose to meet this need. The Sthree Toilet was set up at the Majestic bus terminal of the Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation (KSRTC) . Built from a scrap vehicle, it serves women exclusively. The toilet has three Indian-style and two Western-style commodes . A sanitary napkin vending machine and an incinerator support menstrual hygiene. A dedicated space lets mothers feed their babies and change diapers. Sensor lights run on solar power generated by the facility itself . Waste drains into the nearest sewage chamber at the bus station. The toilet has proved especially helpful for mothers travelling with young children. Navi Mumbai’s Sustainable Toilets: A Model of Eco-Conscious Urban Design Can a public toilet be built from what a city throws away? Navi Mumbai has shown that it can. The Navi Mumbai Municipal Corporation (NMMC) has developed Aspirational Toilets at Sector 14, Koparkhairane. The site lies near the Nisargudyan urban garden, a busy public space. Around 8,000 to 9,000 visitors use the facility every day. The structure uses 426 square metres of recycled plastic sheeting . This includes 5.3 metric tonnes of single-use plastic , 11,700 plastic bottles and 35,200 bottle caps. Builders also reused 85 repurposed computer keyboards and 284 kg of scrap metal . The project puts the principle of Reduce, Reuse and Recycle into everyday practice. Safety and comfort are built into the design. Separate sections for men and women ensure privacy. Units for children and persons with disabilities, baby care stations and sanitary pad vending machines serve all users. A fountain running on treated sewage water completes its green design. The complex now stands as a symbol of environmental innovation and civic pride. Swachh Smart Toilets: Freshrooms Bring Comfort to Bhopal Shoppers, vendors and commuters crowd Bhopal’s 10 Number Market every day. The Bhopal Municipal Corporation has set up ‘Freshrooms’, smart and luxury public convenience centres . They follow a Design-Build-Operate-Transfer (DBOT) model under a Public-Private Partnership (PPP) . The Smart Lounge at the market covers 800 to 1,000 square feet. It serves 500 to 1,000 visitors daily . Technology lies at the heart of the facility. It offers sensor-based toilets and touch-free urinals . Visitors can also use hot and cold showers, lockers and Wi-Fi. A café, vending machines and baby-changing rooms add to the comfort. A digital information wall keeps users informed. Separate, accessible facilities serve men, women and persons with disabilities. By integrating technology, comfort and sustainability, Freshrooms demonstrate how innovative models can deliver world-class sanitation while ensuring financial self-sufficiency . Smart Sanitary Solutions in Karad: Safe Disposal, Safer City Clean toilets are one part of the sanitation story. Safe disposal of sanitary waste is another. Used napkins and diapers, if dumped openly, harm health and the environment. Stigma often keeps the issue hidden. Karad , a small city in Satara district of Maharashtra , has tackled this challenge head-on. It ensures 100% segregation, collection and processing of sanitary and biomedical waste. Nearly 300 to 350 kg of sanitary waste is collected daily from hospitals, clinics, households and other facilities. The first step was to break the taboo around sanitary waste. Workshops, community outreach and public announcements explained the risks of careless disposal. The Karad Municipal Council (KMC) worked with women residents to form awareness groups. These groups carried the message across residential areas. Separate red bins were placed in public toilets to make safe disposal easier for women. Schools were encouraged to install sanitary pad vending machines and disposal systems. The city’s Information, Education and Communication (IEC) team urged users to wrap used pads in paper. Many schools have since installed incinerators. Their residue goes to the biomedical waste treatment plant. Garbage collection vehicles carry a separate bin for sanitary waste . Staff sort this waste so that only suitable material reaches the incinerator. KMC has partnered with the Karad Hospital Association to treat this waste. KMC allocated land for construction of the biomedical waste treatment plant, while the association operates and maintains it. This is a 600 kg/day Common Biomedical Waste Treatment Facility (CBWTF) . It processes the sanitary waste collected by the council free of charge. Its central incinerator reaches temperatures of up to 1,200°C . Gases are filtered to remove harmful substances. Emissions are monitored in real time and linked to the State Pollution Control Board (SPCB) system. This PPP partnership has eased the council’s financial burden, as it bears only collection and transport costs. High-temperature incineration of sanitary waste has reduced health risks and protects sanitation workers handling the waste. Open dumping has been eliminated, preventing environmental contamination and reducing the spread of diseases. It has improved residents’ quality of life, particularly for women affected by sanitary waste disposal challenges. Comfort, Cleanliness & Care for Tirupati’s Pilgrims Places of faith draw lakhs of visitors, making clean toilets a daily necessity. Tirupati is among India’s busiest pilgrimage destinations. The Tirupati Municipal Corporation has built modern toilet complexes for devotees, tourists and residents. A dedicated Pink Toilet Complex for women stands near the bus station. It links key points such as Srinivasam, Vishnuvasam, the railway station and the bus terminal. Women can use Indian and Western toilets, restrooms, and mother care and changing rooms. Incinerators and sanitary napkin vending machines support menstrual hygiene. The complex serves 12,000 to 15,000 users daily . A structured three-shift cleaning system maintains the facility. A Common Public Toilet Complex near the railway station caters to 20,000–25,000 devotees visiting the Govindarajaswamy Temple area daily. Designed for universal access, it provides dedicated facilities for men, women, transgender persons, Divyaang, and children. Ramps, handrails, child-friendly fixtures, and bathing rooms ensure greater comfort, hygiene, and accessibility for pilgrims . Road Ahead Under SBM-U 2.0, the focus has moved beyond building toilets. The goal now is to keep them clean, safe, inclusive and sustainable. These stories show how cities are reaching that goal in their own ways. A scrap bus, recycled plastic, sensor-based fixtures and a high-temperature incinerator each play a part. Partnerships with private operators, hospitals and communities keep these facilities running well. Dedicated workers and caretakers give them life every day. As the Swachh Bharat Mission completes twelve years, the direction is clear. Every citizen, whatever their gender, ability or location, deserves a clean and dignified toilet. From markets to monuments, Indian cities are turning that promise into reality. title: Sustainable Urban Waste Management: Lessons from Goa, Gandhinagar, Kakinada and Ghaziabad
excerpt: An overview of innovative waste‑management practices in four Indian cities, their relevance for UPSC exams and the underlying policy framework of the Swachh Bharat Mission.
releaseDate: 02 OCT 2026 12:04PM A city’s growth is visible not only in its buildings and roads, but also in how it responds to everyday challenges. The way waste is handled, communities participate and services are delivered can shape the quality of urban life. The Swachh Bharat Mission has given this everyday transformation a strong foundation across the country. Over time, the focus has moved beyond simply collecting and disposing of waste. Cities are finding ways to recover value from discarded material, encourage responsible habits and make municipal services more efficient. Green practices are also gaining ground as segregation, recycling, reuse and recovery become integral to local systems. Digital monitoring, data-driven systems and better service delivery are helping local bodies to work with greater precision. These efforts are gradually creating urban spaces that balance environmental responsibility with the needs of everyday life. Cities Leading the Way in Sustainable Urban Transformation Across different regions, cities are demonstrating how local solutions can translate into meaningful environmental outcomes. Their experiences show that sustainable urban transformation can take many forms. These include converting dumping grounds into integrated waste management facilities and promoting zero-waste practices. Technology is also improving everyday sanitation services and strengthening urban systems. The following stories highlight these diverse approaches. A Greener Goa: Turning Waste into Energy Located in the valleys of Saligao, Goa, the Integrated Waste Management Facility Center promotes environmental sustainability. Spread across 113,000 square metres , it is operated by the Goa Waste Management Corporation (GWMC). The facility was formerly used as a garbage dump. It has now been transformed into an integrated, eco-friendly waste management hub for Goa. The center manages 250 metric tons of wet and dry waste every day. At this plant, organic matter is separated from waste and converted into biogas, which helps generate electricity . This energy supports the needs of the local community by alleviating power shortages in the area. Wet waste from restaurants is converted into valuable bioproducts, including methane-rich biogas. Recyclable materials are recovered from 100 metric tons of dry waste processed at the facility. The remaining dry waste is sent to cement factories for co-processing. Additionally, 1.32 kilowatts of electricity is generated from wet waste at the facility. This electricity powers 35 units, with half supplied to the Goa Electricity Department. The plant also generates 7–8 tons of compost daily. Local panchayats use this compost for gardening and reforestation projects. The integrated solid waste management facility is strengthening Goa’s waste management system, processing approximately one-third of the state's total waste . People who once merely collected waste are now part of the plant's trained workforce. This provides livelihood opportunities for several families in the region while benefiting the environment. The plant operates continuously throughout the year, aiming to make the city "zero waste”. Gandhinagar’s Zero-Waste Journey: Citizens Driving Change Gandhinagar in Gujarat stands as a strong example of swachhata and sustainability. Through its commitment to the Swachh Bharat Mission and participation in Swachh Survekshan, the city promotes a culture of cleanliness. Inspired by the global Zero Waste Week movement, the Gandhinagar Municipal Corporation organised impactful activities from 2 nd to 7 th September, 2026. These initiatives aimed to encourage behavioural change and promote the 3R principles: Reduce, Reuse and Recycle . Activities were conducted at 25 locations across the city, directly engaging more than 600 citizens. Targeted social media campaigns further reached and sensitised over 40,000 individuals during the week. The My Theli stalls became vibrant spaces for community participation and sustainable action across Gandhinagar. Citizens were encouraged to donate used clothes. Skilled women from local self-help groups transformed these donations into reusable carry bags. The “ Swachhata Se Shuruvat ” campaign was launched to encourage responsible practices among school students. Quiz competitions were organised to raise awareness about environmental concerns and responsible practices. Engaging and interactive games were designed through which students gained practical insights into sustainability. The Reduce, Reuse, Recycle van visited residents at their doorsteps to collect old clothes, plastic and electronic waste. Participants received rewards for their donations, encouraging greater community involvement. Citizens were also invited to share their personal efforts and daily practices through online testimonials. Through these initiatives, Gandhinagar is advancing its zero-waste vision. The city continues to strengthen resource-conscious practices while working towards the goal of Garbage Free Cities. Kakinada’s Smart Approach to Efficient Waste Management In Andhra Pradesh’s East Godavari District, Kakinada has emerged as a notable example of technology-enabled waste management. Kakinada generates around 144 tons of waste daily, comprising wet, dry and hazardous materials. The Kakinada Municipal Corporation manages this operation across 50 wards, which are further divided into 382 micro pockets. Each micro pocket covers 250 to 350 households and is managed by two sanitation workers. With around 112,993 households , over 973 sanitation workers have been employed to manage waste. These households are strategically organised into 40,661 designated waste collection points across the city. Digital tools are used to streamline waste collection and transportation. The Online Waste Management System (OWMS) tracks the process in real time. Radio Frequency Identification (RFID), facial recognition, GPS and a human resource management system (HRMS) further support workforce and transportation management. RFID chip-enabled tags are installed at the gates of every waste generator. Collectors scan these tags when waste is picked up. The scanned information is recorded in the OWMS, enabling officials to monitor collection progress. Continuous monitoring and dedicated sanitation staff have helped the system achieve 100% door-to-door collection . The Municipal Corporation has deployed 108 hopper vehicles equipped with GPS tracking devices. These monitor the transportation and report deviations during waste collection and transportation to processing plants. It has also introduced a Facial Recognition System (FRS) for all SafaiMitras. Workers can now record their attendance using facial recognition technology. This eliminates the need for manual attendance registers or fingerprint scanners. All these technologies are integrated into a Central Command Centre for close monitoring. Around 60% of residents now segregate waste at source. The combined efforts of sanitation workers and residents are strengthening Kakinada’s ability to manage its waste efficiently. Ghaziabad: Turning Waste into Carbon Value Ghaziabad, Uttar Pradesh, is advancing cleanliness and urban development while taking steps to reduce carbon emissions. The Ghaziabad Municipal Corporation (GMC) has registered for an international carbon credit project. The initiative is verified by the United Nations and combines environmental protection with potential financial benefits. Improved solid waste management under the Swachh Bharat Mission can reduce greenhouse gases such as methane from dumping sites. Greater use of clean fuels and energy sources can also lower dependence on fossil fuels and reduce carbon emissions. In line with these efforts, the Ghaziabad Municipal Corporation has demonstrated its commitment to the Sustainable Development Goals. It has been accredited under the Verified Carbon Standard (VCS) , supported by the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC). The GMC has replaced old streetlights across the city with energy-efficient LED lights. This measure reduces carbon emissions while also lowering electricity consumption. It is also adopting "wet waste composting" to produce compost from wet waste. This process supports faster waste management and helps reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Following Indore in Madhya Pradesh, Ghaziabad is set to become the first urban local body (ULB) in Uttar Pradesh and the second in the country to turn waste into a new source of value. Together, these measures are expected to reduce carbon dioxide emissions by approximately 2.7 lakh tonnes . This reduction corresponds to 2.7 lakh carbon credits , with one tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent to one credit. Certified credits can be converted into revenue by being sold on the international carbon market. The initiative supports cleanliness, environmental protection and economic opportunities for Ghaziabad. Building Cities That Value Every Resource The transformation underway across cities reflects a broader shift in the way urban resources are managed. Technology is strengthening everyday sanitation services while citizens are becoming active participants in sustainable practices. Local solutions are creating visible improvements in everyday urban life. They also show the value of combining innovation with people’s efforts for effective waste management.
